def: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Train a reward model on preference comparisons, then optimize a policy against it. The ChatGPT-era alignment technique; for reasoning, often replaced by RLVR.
Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards. Reward comes from a programmatic checker (math answer match, code unit tests pass), not a learned reward model. The R1/o1-era recipe.
Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback. Reward is generated by an LLM-as-judge. Cheap proxy for human labels; debated for reasoning.
Group Relative Policy Optimization. PPO variant from the DeepSeekMath paper. Computes advantages as group-relative normalizations over G samples per prompt — no value head needed.
Direct Preference Optimization. Closed-form alternative to RLHF that learns directly from pairwise preferences, no reward model.
Proximal Policy Optimization. Trust-region policy gradient with a clipped surrogate. Pre-2025 standard; largely displaced by GRPO for reasoning.
Classical Monte-Carlo policy gradient. Several 2024–25 reasoning RL papers report comparable results to GRPO with plain REINFORCE plus variance-reduction tricks.
Trained by RL from a base model with no SFT seed. Demonstrated by DeepSeek that reasoning behavior can emerge without CoT demonstrations.
R1-Zero followed by SFT-then-RL refinement to fix readability and language-mixing. The capability is in R1-Zero; R1 is cosmetic refinement.
SFT-style examples used to initialize an RL run. For R1, a few thousand high-quality CoT demonstrations curated for tone.
Train a smaller student on chains generated by a larger reasoning teacher (e.g. R1-Distill-Qwen-7B). More parameter-efficient than running RLVR directly on the small model.
Outcome Reward Model. Scores entire trajectories by final-answer correctness. Cheaper to label, lower-signal than a PRM.
Process Reward Model. Scores each intermediate step. Per Lightman et al. (2023), PRMs train more effective verifiers than ORMs at equal label budget.
Heuristic that assigns step-level labels by Monte-Carlo rollout: a step is "good" if rollouts from it reach the correct final answer.
RL using only binary final-answer correctness as reward, no learned verifier in the loop. R1-Zero is the canonical example.
Supervised Fine-Tuning. Cross-entropy training on (prompt, completion) pairs. Common precursor to RL for reasoning.
Chain of Thought. The string of intermediate tokens between question and final answer.
Original (Nye et al. 2021) name for intermediate-token reasoning. Interchangeable with CoT today; survives in learnability theory.
Eliciting CoT without exemplars, typically via "Let's think step by step" (Kojima et al. 2022).
Eliciting CoT by including worked examples in the prompt (Wei et al. 2022).
Sample K chains independently, take majority-vote answer (Wang et al. 2022). Cheap, effective, no verifier.
Sample N chains, score with a verifier, return the highest-scoring. Strictly stronger than self-consistency when the verifier is informative.
Total inference-time FLOPs (or tokens, as proxy) spent on a single question, including sampling, search, verification.
Empirical regularity that accuracy on reasoning tasks grows roughly log-linearly with inference-time compute, up to a task-dependent saturation.
Capping the number of tokens a model may emit before being forced to answer. Used in s1 (Muennighoff 2025) to study and improve scaling curves.
Two complementary failure modes. Refusal-to-think: perfunctory chain on easy tasks. Refusal-to-stop: enormous chain that exhausts the budget without answering.
Monte-Carlo Tree Search where nodes are partial CoT prefixes and edges are next-step extensions. Used in some post-training search systems.
Yao et al. (2023). Explicit tree search over CoT branches with a heuristic value function (often the model rating its own partial chains).
Besta et al. (2023). Generalizes ToT to DAGs with explicit aggregation operators.
Sample multiple chains, summarize them into a new prompt, recurse. Trades depth for branching.
Use a small draft model to propose tokens that the large model verifies in parallel. Orthogonal to reasoning but relevant — long CoT shifts the cost balance.
The draft-and-verify idea applied at the level of reasoning steps rather than tokens.
American Invitational Mathematics Examination. 15-question, integer-answer math contest. AIME-24/25/26 are canonical reasoning leaderboards.
500-problem subset of MATH (Hendrycks 2021), standardized by Lightman et al. (2023). Saturating in mid-2025.
Grade-school math word problems (Cobbe et al. 2021). Largely saturated; still a calibration baseline.
Python function-completion benchmark (Chen et al. 2021). Heavily saturated; superseded by LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench Verified.
Periodically refreshed coding benchmark with date cutoffs to mitigate train-test contamination.
Human-validated subset of SWE-bench — real GitHub issues with known passing patches. Reasoning models post substantial gains over non-reasoning siblings.
Epoch AI benchmark of original research-level math problems. Single-digit % accuracy even for frontier reasoners as of early 2026.
Chollet's abstraction-and-reasoning benchmarks. ARC-AGI-3 launched 2026-03-25 with a new generation-and-search structure.
Humanity's Last Exam. Multi-domain expert-level benchmark (CAIS / Scale, late 2024). Designed to remain hard after benchmark saturation.
Graduate-level Google-Proof Q&A (Rein et al. 2023). 200-question expert-validated subset; the standard "PhD-level science" benchmark.
Competitive-programming rating, used as a continuous-valued reasoning benchmark by OpenAI in their o1/o3 reports.
Probability that at least one of k sampled completions is correct. Standard coding metric; relates to but distinct from best-of-N.
Constant-depth threshold circuits with polynomial size. Where log-precision transformers are believed to live in a single forward pass; many "hard" reasoning problems lie outside.
T tokens of CoT extends a constant-depth transformer to roughly T-step serial computation (Li et al. 2024; Merrill & Sabharwal 2024).
Hypothesis that RL-trained reasoners encode a search procedure into their sampling distribution, so greedy decoding mimics what an external search would do.
CoT generation as implicit posterior inference over a latent "solution program." Extends ICL-as-Bayes (Xie 2022) to multi-step.
A CoT is the source code of a program the model is "compiling" to its answer. Implies non-CoT inference interprets compiled artifacts of similar programs from training.
A CoT is faithful iff the visible chain is causally responsible for the answer. Operationalized via truncation, paraphrase, and step-injection tests (Lanham et al. 2023).
An unfaithful CoT: the model answers via a route other than the visible chain, then emits the chain as a plausible justification. Documented frequently (Turpin 2023).
A model deliberately performing worse than its capability would predict, typically to hide a capability.
A model behaving as if aligned during evaluation but differently under perceived deployment. Distinct from sandbagging in motivation.
Long CoTs hurting accuracy on tasks where shorter chains suffice (Chen et al. 2024). Canonical example: "2 + 3 = ?" eliciting a 200-token chain.
A reasoning model emitting tens of thousands of tokens without committing to an answer. A practical resource issue.
An early hallucinated step that subsequent steps confidently build on. Mechanism described in Bachmann & Nagarajan (2024).
A teacher-forced learner exploiting next-token correlations that don't reflect the target computation (Bachmann & Nagarajan 2024).
Reasoning model switching languages mid-chain. Documented in R1-Zero; partially fixed by R1's SFT pass.
Policy finds a reward shortcut the verifier accepts. For math, often by emitting a final answer that pattern-matches a substring rather than computing.
Policy concentrates on a narrow distribution, losing exploration. Partially mitigated by GRPO's group-relative normalization.
